Pregnancy

Germander in pregnancy: Teucrium polium, liver risk and exposure advice

Updated: October 19, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Teucrium polium is sold or discussed as an herbal remedy for digestion, blood sugar and many other concerns. During pregnancy, the important issue is not how long it has been used, but whether a particular preparation has a worthwhile benefit and acceptable safety. Serious liver injury has been reported in people using this plant, including around childbirth. Avoid taking it as a remedy in pregnancy; if you have already used it, stop the product and seek advice rather than assuming either that a small amount is safe or that harm is inevitable.

Know which plant and product are being discussed

The name in this article is Teucrium polium L., a species of germander in the mint family, Lamiaceae. Kew currently accepts it as a subshrub native to the western Mediterranean. Common names such as felty, golden or mountain germander, and regional names such as kalpoureh, do not reliably identify every product. Older medical literature and local usage can apply names more broadly than a current botanical classification.

Other germanders, including Teucrium chamaedrys and Teucrium capitatum, are separate species. Some also have liver-injury reports, but their findings are not an identical dose-and-risk profile for T. polium. A hairy leaf, flower colour, seller’s description or photograph cannot confirm a package’s identity, contents or safety. Keep the scientific name, ingredient list and packaging for a professional to examine; do not forage from an online description.

Traditional use is a starting point for research

Traditional claims include easing stomach upset, gas, diarrhoea and cramps; reducing inflammation, pain and fever; controlling blood sugar or weight; and treating bacterial or fungal infections. Other claims concern dental decay, abscesses and mouth ulcers, gallbladder and urinary problems, asthma and other respiratory symptoms, wound healing, memory, energy and nerves. Claims also extend to children’s rickets, cancer or heart-attack prevention, liver protection, menstrual symptoms and starting labour. This range is a list of claimed uses, not a set of established treatment indications.

Plant chemicals and antioxidant, antimicrobial or anti-inflammatory activity in a laboratory do not establish clinical benefit or pregnancy safety. Some human research exists: a small trial tested a topical preparation added to standard care for non-infected diabetic foot ulcers, and another studied menstrual bleeding in young adults. Neither establishes that swallowing a tea or extract during pregnancy is safe, treats all these conditions or benefits a baby. Results from a specific preparation and route cannot validate every product sold under the same name.

Do not use it to replace care for a specific problem

Digestive discomfort, pain or fever deserves advice appropriate to its cause and pregnancy stage. Do not use germander to treat a dental abscess, urinary or vaginal infection, asthma attack or other breathing problem, or to postpone assessment. Antimicrobial activity in a dish does not show that a home preparation reaches an infection safely or replaces an antibiotic, dental treatment or inhaler when needed.

Likewise, do not replace diabetes treatment, attempt weight loss in pregnancy with germander, or use it for cancer, cardiovascular prevention or a child’s bone disease. Proposed liver-protective effects in experimental models are especially misleading beside documented human liver injury. Evidence-based care can address the original symptom without requiring you to accept the risks of an unproven herbal regimen.

Human liver injury is the clearest serious warning

Published T. polium reports describe hepatitis after tea, powder or extract use. A 2007 report described two people with marked liver-enzyme elevations after taking it; stopping the product was followed by recovery. A separate case series described three women with serious liver injury presenting after childbirth, with exposure during pregnancy or the postpartum period. Some had similar problems after previous use. These reports support a real safety concern; they do not tell us how often injury occurs.

The official LiverTox review also records severe germander-related liver failure, including a T. polium report requiring transplantation. Recovery after stopping is common in reported cases, but cannot be promised, and restarting can provoke further injury. Do not test whether a suspected reaction returns, switch to another germander preparation as an experiment, or try to treat the liver with another herbal product. Liver symptoms require medical assessment.

Pregnancy findings must be interpreted by study type

There is no established pregnancy-specific benefit or reliably defined safe dose of T. polium. One experiment exposed developing chicken embryos directly to plant extract and found serious effects on survival and blood-vessel development. That is a warning from a nonhuman model, not a study of pregnant people drinking tea. Its results cannot be converted into a human miscarriage percentage, a prediction of malformations or a claim that one exposure will end a pregnancy.

Traditional descriptions of bringing on periods or labour also do not establish a safe or effective induction method, or prove a particular human uterine effect. Avoid using the plant to start bleeding, induce labour or treat a suspected miscarriage. The small postpartum case series reported apparently well infants, but was not designed to establish fetal safety. Both maternal liver toxicity and uncertain reproductive evidence matter; neither justifies reassurance about a small dose.

Preparation, amount and other medicines change the question

Tea is not automatically a mild or safe form: human liver-injury reports include tea preparations. Powders, concentrated extracts, essential oils and mixed products are not interchangeable. There is no validated home spoonful, dilution, boiling time or course that makes T. polium a pregnancy-safe remedy. Product strength, species identity, contaminants and additional ingredients may be uncertain; taking it for longer is not a way to demonstrate tolerance.

Tell the pharmacist or maternity clinician about every medicine and supplement, particularly if you have liver or kidney disease or are treated for diabetes or another ongoing condition. Herbal interactions may be incompletely documented, so an absent interaction warning is not proof of compatibility. Do not stop an essential prescription to make room for the herb. After childbirth, do not assume it safely increases milk supply: pregnancy and breastfeeding safety are different questions, and the postpartum liver reports remain relevant.

What to do if you have already taken it

Stop taking the germander product and contact your maternity team, clinician, pharmacist or local poison-advice service promptly for an individual assessment. Keep the package or a safe sample, and note the scientific and common names, ingredients, form, estimated amount, timing, number of doses, pregnancy stage and any symptoms. A single exposure does not by itself establish that you or your baby have been harmed; a reassuring feeling also cannot rule out a delayed problem.

If you suspect poisoning or a harmful exposure, get immediate medical help; if you are unsure whether the product is harmful, obtain urgent poison or medical advice rather than waiting for symptoms. Follow the service’s instructions. Do not make yourself vomit, take a home antidote or charcoal, or eat or drink something as a counter-remedy while waiting for poisoning care. Keep medicines and herbal packages available for the treating team.

Liver symptoms and general emergencies

Yellowing of the eyes or skin needs urgent medical assessment, even without pain; dark urine, pale stools, itching, nausea or unusual fatigue may accompany it. Persistent vomiting or significant new abdominal symptoms also need prompt advice after exposure. These symptoms are not a diagnosis of germander toxicity: pregnancy-related liver disorders, infections, gallbladder disease and other causes may need to be considered.

Loss of consciousness, a seizure, severe breathing difficulty or sudden confusion needs emergency care immediately. Severe or worsening pelvic or lower abdominal pain, pain that hurts with movement or touch, or pelvic pain with faintness, dizziness, shoulder-tip pain, breathing difficulty or heavy vaginal bleeding also needs emergency care. Do not drive yourself or wait for a routine appointment. A fast heartbeat, dry mouth or constipation alone does not identify the substance or reliably grade the severity of poisoning.

Pregnancy assessment and follow-up are individual

Contact maternity care urgently for any vaginal bleeding during pregnancy; heavy bleeding or bleeding with severe abdominal pain, shoulder pain, faintness or loss of consciousness is an emergency. New pelvic pain with a possible pregnancy needs urgent assessment even without a previous positive test. Once you know your baby’s usual movement pattern, reduced, absent or changed movements need immediate maternity contact, without waiting until the next day.

The team may assess your symptoms, examine the product history and arrange liver tests or other investigations when indicated. Results and the pregnancy stage guide follow-up; there is no universal scan or blood-test schedule for every reported exposure. Keep routine antenatal appointments and seek help for the reason you originally considered the herb. A history of use should be shared openly, without blame, so care can be based on the actual exposure.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Keep the exact product and exposure details and tell the maternity clinician or pharmacist why you took it; ask about appropriate treatment for that concern.

Stop germander use and seek an individual assessment rather than relying on a small-dose claim, laboratory benefit or a different species’ information.

Agree on any necessary follow-up and act promptly on jaundice, pregnancy bleeding or emergency symptoms; do not retry the herb or use a home antidote.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help organise product names, exposure dates, symptoms and questions for a consultation. It cannot identify a plant or mixture, diagnose liver injury, calculate a fetus’s risk or decide which tests or treatment you need. A record or reassuring app entry must not delay medical or maternity care.

When to seek help

Avoid Teucrium polium remedies during pregnancy and do not use them for labour induction or to replace prescribed care. After exposure, stop the product and seek prompt professional advice; suspected poisoning needs immediate medical help. Yellow eyes or skin require urgent assessment. Loss of consciousness, seizures, severe breathing difficulty, sudden confusion, severe or worsening pelvic pain or pelvic pain with faintness, dizziness, shoulder-tip pain, breathing difficulty or heavy bleeding require emergency care. Do not drive yourself, induce vomiting or use a home antidote. Contact maternity care urgently for pregnancy bleeding and immediately for reduced or changed usual baby movements.

Evidence notes updated: October 19, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Avoid taking Teucrium polium as a remedy during pregnancy; a safe small dose has not been established.
  • Human liver-injury reports include tea and pregnancy or postpartum exposure; a natural label does not remove that concern.
  • Chicken-embryo findings cannot predict a human pregnancy outcome or prove harm from one exposure.
  • Traditional claims and small route-specific studies do not establish broad treatment benefits or oral pregnancy safety.
  • Stop the product after exposure, keep its details and seek advice; jaundice and emergency warning signs need prompt appropriate care.

Frequently asked questions

What benefits are traditionally claimed for germander?

Claims cover digestion, pain and inflammation, blood sugar, infections, dental and respiratory problems, wounds and wider preventive or reproductive effects. They should not be read as established clinical benefits. Limited studies of specific preparations do not validate the whole list or show that oral use is safe in pregnancy.

Does Teucrium polium have a proven benefit during pregnancy?

An established pregnancy-specific benefit has not been demonstrated. Laboratory activity or an adult topical-wound study cannot establish a safe pregnancy treatment. Ask for appropriate care for the symptom instead of using germander to replace a prescription or delay assessment.

Is a small amount or weak tea safe?

No pregnancy-safe amount, dilution or course has been established. Tea preparations appear in human liver-injury reports, and strength and identity may be uncertain. Avoid taking it; if exposure has already happened, stop the product and obtain individual advice without assuming inevitable harm.

Can it cause miscarriage or fetal abnormalities?

Nonhuman developmental findings raise concern, but do not quantify human miscarriage, premature-birth or malformation risks. The chicken-embryo experiment was not a pregnant-human trial. An exposure history alone cannot predict the outcome; discuss the actual product, timing and symptoms with maternity or poison-advice professionals.

What adverse effects are most important?

Serious hepatitis and, in severe reports, liver failure are important concerns. Other symptoms such as vomiting, abdominal discomfort or a changed heartbeat need assessment in context rather than being treated as a reliable germander-specific checklist. Yellow eyes or skin need urgent care; loss of consciousness, seizures or severe breathing difficulty need emergency care.

Can I use it to start labour or bleeding?

Do not use it to induce labour, bring on bleeding or manage a suspected miscarriage. Traditional reproductive uses do not establish effectiveness or safety. Pregnancy bleeding and pain need clinical assessment, with emergency care for heavy bleeding, severe or worsening pain or associated faintness, shoulder pain or breathing difficulty.

Is it safer after birth for digestion or milk supply?

Do not assume this. Serious liver-injury reports include postpartum use for digestion or milk-supply reasons. Breastfeeding safety and benefit are not established by traditional use. Ask the maternity, primary-care or feeding team for an assessment of digestive symptoms or milk transfer and supply concerns.

What should I bring when asking about an exposure?

Bring the packaging or safe sample, ingredient and plant names, form and strength if known, estimated amount and timing, pregnancy stage, symptoms and all other medicines. Stop the product and obtain prompt advice. Suspected poisoning or emergency symptoms need immediate help; do not induce vomiting or use a home counter-remedy.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
